name: Cabeus
short: Water measured in the LCROSS impact plume at one spot.

evidence.finding: LCROSS measured water in debris blasted from one impact site in Cabeus; this does not confirm ice across the crater.
evidence.citation: Colaprete, A., et al. (2010). Detection of water in the LCROSS ejecta plume. Science 330, 463-468. doi:10.1126/science.1186986.

evidence.finding: M3 reported signs of surface ice in small permanently shaded patches inside this crater.
evidence.citation: Li, S., Lucey, P.G., Milliken, R.E., Hayne, P.O., Fisher, E., Williams, J.-P., Hurley, D.M., Elphic, R.C. (2018). positionNote: Marker at the LCROSS Centaur impact, not the crater centre; the diameter describes Cabeus.

name: Amundsen
short: Cold traps are predicted here; no detection is mapped here.

evidence.instrument: LRO Diviner thermal model and LOLA shadow model
evidence.finding: Temperature and shadow maps predict cold traps here, but the reviewed map of reported ice signals has no detection assigned to this crater.
evidence.citation: Paige, D.A., et al. (2010). Diviner Lunar Radiometer observations of cold traps in the Moon's south polar region. Science 330, 479-482. doi:10.1126/science.1187726. name: Peary
short: Radar signs seen from orbit; ice is possible, not measured here.

evidence.finding: Radar found unusual signals in small craters inside Peary that may come from buried ice. Rough ground also changes radar signals; no water was measured on the spot, and this is not a claim about the whole crater.
evidence.citation: ISRO (2020). Chandrayaan-2 completes a year around the Moon, pp. 9–10, Figure 9. See also Bussey, D.B.J., Spudis, P.D., and the Mini-RF Team (2011). New insights into lunar processes and history from global mapping by Mini-RF radar. LPSC 42, abstract 2086.

evidence.finding: The Mini-RF team described radar signals consistent with possible ice in permanently shaded small craters inside Peary. These are orbital signs with more than one possible cause.
evidence.citation: Bussey, D.B.J., Spudis, P.D., and the Mini-RF Team (2011). New insights into lunar processes and history from global mapping by Mini-RF radar. LPSC 42, abstract 2086.

positionNote: Marker at the named crater centre for context, not at every possible deposit.

name: Rozhdestvenskiy
short: Radar signs seen from orbit; ice is possible, not measured here.

evidence.finding: Radar found unusual signals in small craters inside Rozhdestvenskiy that may come from buried ice. Rough ground can give similar signals; no water was measured on the spot, and this is not a claim about the whole crater.
evidence.citation: NASA/GSFC/JHUAPL. Mini RF Rozhdestvenskiy. Bussey, D.B.J., Spudis, P.D., and the Mini-RF Team (2011). New insights into lunar processes and history from global mapping by Mini-RF radar. LPSC 42, abstract 2086. Spudis et al. (2010), GRL 37, L06204, doi:10.1029/2009GL042259.

evidence.finding: A high radar polarisation ratio can come from rough rock or from ice. The instrument does not directly measure water in the ground.
evidence.citation: NASA (2010). NASA Radar Finds Ice Deposits at Moon’s North Pole, 2 March 2010; the article explains that circular polarisation ratio is not uniquely diagnostic of roughness or ice.

positionNote: Marker at the named crater centre for context, not at every possible deposit.

name: Hermite
short: Radar signs seen from orbit; ice is possible, not measured here.

evidence.finding: Mini-RF reported unusual radar signals in small craters on Hermite’s floor. A scattering model favours possible buried ice, but roughness can affect the signal; no water was measured on the spot.
evidence.citation: Spudis, P.D., et al. (2013). Evidence for water ice on the Moon: Results for anomalous polar craters from the LRO Mini-RF imaging radar. JGR Planets 118, 2016–2029, Table 3 and Figure 7. doi:10.1002/jgre.20156.

evidence.instrument: LRO Diviner temperature measurements and LOLA shadow models
evidence.finding: Diviner measured very cold ground in Hermite, and LOLA models show lasting shadow in part of its south-western floor. Cold and shadow allow possible ice storage; they do not measure water.
evidence.citation: NASA/GSFC/JHUAPL. Hermite Crater; Diviner temperature observations and LOLA long-term illumination modelling. See also NASA LRO, Taking the Moon’s Temperature.

positionNote: Marker at the named crater centre for context, not at every possible deposit.

name: Erlanger
short: Radar signs seen from orbit; ice is possible, not measured here.

evidence.finding: Mini-RF reported unusual radar signals inside Erlanger. A scattering model favours possible buried ice, but roughness can affect the signal; no water was measured on the spot.
evidence.citation: Spudis, P.D., et al. (2013). Evidence for water ice on the Moon: Results for anomalous polar craters from the LRO Mini-RF imaging radar. JGR Planets 118, 2016–2029, Table 3. doi:10.1002/jgre.20156.

evidence.finding: LROC shows that much of Erlanger’s floor stays in permanent shadow. Shadow can help ice last in suitable cold patches; the photograph alone is not an ice detection.
evidence.citation: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University (2009). Eternal Darkness Near the North Pole, PIA12899. LROC Permanently Shadowed Regions Atlas, Erlanger entry NP_869610_0287570.

positionNote: Marker at the named crater centre for context, not at every possible deposit.

name: Bosch
short: Cold ground could keep ice; this marker is a prediction.

evidence.finding: NASA lists Bosch among the very cold northern craters that could trap water ice. This is a prediction from cold conditions, not a measurement of water at this crater.
evidence.citation: Borowski, S.K., et al. (2018). Robust Exploration and Commercial Missions to the Moon Using Nuclear Thermal Rocket Propulsion and In Situ Propellants Derived from Lunar Polar Ice Deposits. NASA/TM—2018-219937, p. 7 and Figure 4(b).

positionNote: Marker at the named crater centre for context, not at every possible deposit.
